prompt.context: We have been contacted by a large distilled spirits manufacturing and marketing company to develop a new strategy for one of their brands. The scotch industry was introduced in North America in the early 1940s and grew steadily until the 1960s. The industry has subsequently declined in volume every year to 1996 at a rate of about 3% per year. From 1996-1998, the volume declined at only 1% per year. Our client participates only in the premium segment with one brand, tied as the #2 brand with 25% market share of volume (#1 has 35%, #2 has 25%, we have 25%, #4 has 10%, others have 5%). Our brand is priced slightly above the industry average (10%).
prompt.question: Develop a new strategy for the client's scotch brand. As part of your analysis: (1) define strategy, (2) outline a process to develop a new strategy, (3) diagnose why the scotch market has been declining, (4) assess the brand's competitive position, and (5) recommend the best path forward to maximize profit.

clarifying_info.q: How is the scotch market segmented?
clarifying_info.a: There are three segments: low-end (e.g., private label CVS whisky), premium (typically seen on the back bar in a bar), and super-premium (including Chivas Regal and single malt scotches).

clarifying_info.q: What are the sizes of the segments?
clarifying_info.a: 40% of the volume in low-end, 50% in premium, and 10% in super-premium.
Yes, all segments are economically profitable.
20% in low-end, 60% in premium, 20% in super-premium.

clarifying_info.q: What are customer needs in this market?
clarifying_info.a: Taste (blind preference or perceived quality via color/thickness), Fashion (is it fashionable to drink), and Badge (does the brand make me feel important/different/mature/sophisticated).
#1 has gained share from us, the #4 and other brands, but mostly from us. #2 has held share.

clarifying_info.q: How profitable are we relative to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: We all have the same cost of goods; differences are in selling costs and advertising costs. #1 has highest selling and advertising costs, then #2, then #3. #1 and we have a price premium; #2 is at industry average; #3 and others are slightly below average.

clarifying_info.q: What do customers think of our brand attributes?
clarifying_info.a: We have a disadvantaged taste, disadvantaged badge, but competitive fashion.
We actually have advantaged distribution relative to competitors.
People remember our advertising — awareness is not the problem.
Very poor advertising effectiveness — customers remember our ads but are not convinced to buy.

We spend about 25% too little money; we spend heavily on billboards which are cheap but don't reach the right audience; we spend too much at Christmas for impulse buyers and miss brand-loyal buyers; our advertising copy has been poor while #1 has had very good campaigns.

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of this brand within the company portfolio?
clarifying_info.a: This brand is only a small part of the company's portfolio.

framework: Participation: geography, customer segment, high-level product segment
Operating Configuration: cost and asset strategy

questions.guidance: A strong answer covers the five elements: (1) Participation — where to play (geography, customer, segment); (2) Offering — what product/service to provide; (3) Pricing — how to price products and services; (4) Operating Configuration — cost/asset structure; (5) Distribution — how to reach customers. These five dimensions together define a complete strategy.

questions.prompt: What would be your process to develop a new strategy?
questions.guidance: Four-step process: (1) Position Assessment — understand sources and drivers of profitability (business profitability, strategies, market economics, competitive position); (2) Alternative Identification — generate strategic options; (3) Alternative Evaluation — assess feasibility, fit, and value of each option; (4) Business Plan — develop a plan to implement the chosen alternative.

questions.prompt: In the first meeting with the client to scope out the project, what would you want to know?
questions.guidance: Key scoping questions: ulterior motives/politics involved; what prior work has been done; what they want to find out; how they want to work together; time constraints; who should be involved; basic brand information (profit, volume, etc.); hypotheses on key issues; thoughts on likely strategic alternatives; key questions that must be answered regardless of strategy.

questions.prompt: What might be some reasons you would NOT want to accept this project?
questions.guidance: Reasons to decline: politics that would undermine objective work; client not committed to value creation; looking for scapegoats rather than solutions; inability to satisfy the business unit manager; generally difficult client relationship.

questions.prompt: What kind of information would you want to understand to determine the reason for the steady volume decline to 1996, explain the 'kink' in the volume decline from 1996-1998, and forecast future market volume?
questions.guidance: The key diagnostic question is: is the decline driven by fewer people drinking scotch, or by existing drinkers consuming less, or both? The answer is fewer people have been drinking scotch. Two factors explain this: (1) general decline in popularity — vodka and wine have gained volume; (2) demographic decline in the 35-50 age group that traditionally drinks scotch. The 'kink' (slowdown from 3% to 1% decline) is explained by baby boomers aging into the 35-50 cohort, expanding that segment. Looking forward, as baby boomers continue to age into the key demographic AND single malt scotch becomes more fashionable, the market should improve.

questions.prompt: What kind of analysis would you complete to quantify the reduction in number of scotch drinkers?
questions.guidance: Six analytical approaches: (1) review census data; (2) complete literature searches; (3) interview customers; (4) interview distribution channel members; (5) interview other producers; (6) complete market research studies; (7) review the client's historical data.

questions.prompt: Would you think the scotch industry is profitable? Explain structurally.
questions.guidance: Yes, the industry is structurally very profitable, though declining volume is eroding total profit. Key structural drivers: high barriers to entry (long time to build a brand); very strong brand loyalty — customers won't switch easily; health perception barrier limits new entrants to the consumer base; taste barrier (hard to acquire); customers are not price sensitive; high regulatory costs/taxes create a further barrier; competitor intensity is low (little price competition, advertising investment is noticeable but not extreme).

questions.prompt: What are your potential hypotheses for why our brand is underperforming relative to competitors?
questions.guidance: Five hypotheses to test: (1) Customers perceive our brand as having poorer ratings on key attributes — TRUE: disadvantaged taste, disadvantaged badge, but competitive fashion; (2) We do not have the same distribution/availability as competitors — FALSE: we have advantaged distribution; (3) We are priced too high relative to our attributes — TRUE; (4) Customers are not aware of our products (advertising awareness) — FALSE: people remember our advertising; (5) Customers are not convinced to buy from our advertising (advertising effectiveness) — TRUE: very poor advertising effectiveness.

questions.prompt: Why has our advertising effectiveness been poor?
questions.guidance: Four root causes: (1) insufficient spending — we spend about 25% too little; (2) wrong media mix — heavy reliance on billboards (cheap but wrong audience); (3) wrong timing — heavy spend at Christmas for impulse buyers, missing brand-loyal buyers during the rest of the year; (4) poor creative/copy — our campaigns have been poor while #1 brand has had very good campaigns.

questions.prompt: How would you determine how much money to spend on the advertising budget?
questions.guidance: Multiple methods: (1) set a target reach and frequency, then back out required investment based on media/timing/quality; (2) spend as much as competitors — note this would require a 100% increase in advertising investment; (3) spend the same % of revenue as competitors; (4) index advertising investment relative to the price premium received (e.g., if #1 brand has a 10% price premium and invests $10MM/year versus industry average of $5MM, and we want a 0% price premium, we invest at the $5MM industry average; if we want a 10% price discount, we invest at $2.5MM); (5) break-even analysis — spend up to the point where additional advertising investment is economically break-even.

math.setup: Indexing advertising to price premium: #1 brand has 10% price premium and invests $10MM/year; industry average advertising spend is $5MM/year. Ratio: $10MM spend for 10% premium = $1MM per 1% premium. For a 0% premium target, invest at industry average ($5MM). For a 10% discount target, invest at $2.5MM (half the industry average).
steps: #1 spends $10MM with a 10% price premium vs. industry average spend of $5MM
Marginal advertising per 1% price premium = ($10MM - $5MM) / 10% = $500K per 1%
For 10% price discount: invest $5MM - (10 x $500K) = $0 (or minimum $2.5MM as floor)
math.answer: Advertising budget indexed to desired price premium; at 0% premium the investment is ~$5MM (industry average); current spend is approximately 25% below required level

questions.prompt: If the goal was to maximize profit (not necessarily maintain share), what are the strategic alternatives, and which offers the greatest profit potential?
questions.guidance: Strategic alternatives: (1) Reformulate the product to change attributes; (2) Change pricing; (3) Reduce costs; (4) Change distribution; (5) Change advertising/promotion strategy; (6) Sell the brand; (7) Milk the brand. The greatest profit potential alternatives: MILK THE BRAND — because market volume is declining so sharply, advertising investment to turn the brand around will never be recovered; reduce investment and harvest cash flow. SELL THE BRAND — the brand's value declines every year as volume falls; selling now captures value before further erosion. INVEST TO BUILD — an alternative is to convince other producers to co-invest in growing the overall scotch category (industry advertising), or link scotch with trends like cigars to shift fashion perception.

questions.prompt: Which strategic alternative will be easiest for the company to implement, and why?
questions.guidance: Key implementation considerations: (1) Is this the largest brand for the company? No — this brand is only a small part of the portfolio, so its decline does not threaten the enterprise; (2) Fit with other brand strategies — if all other portfolio brands are growth brands, milking or selling this one is strategically consistent; (3) Fit with management time and attention — heavy focus on fixing this brand could cause other brands to suffer, offsetting any potential gain. Conclusion: given that market volume is declining steeply and the brand is a small portfolio piece, milking or selling is easiest to implement with least organizational disruption.

brainstorming.prompt: Generate a broad set of strategic alternatives for a declining premium scotch brand seeking to maximize profit.

categories.name: Product/Offering
ideas: Reformulate product to improve taste profile
Introduce single malt variant to capture super-premium growth
Reposition as a cocktail ingredient to attract new consumers

categories.name: Pricing
ideas: Reduce price to industry average to improve value proposition
Use promotional pricing selectively to defend share

categories.name: Advertising & Promotion
ideas: Increase advertising budget by 25%+ to reach required level
Shift media mix away from billboards to targeted channels
Reallocate spend from Christmas to year-round brand-building

categories.name: Distribution
ideas: Leverage advantaged distribution position to gain placement
Focus distribution on on-premise (bars/restaurants) vs. off-premise
Target geographic markets with stronger scotch heritage

categories.name: Portfolio/Corporate
ideas: Sell the brand while it still has value
Milk the brand — harvest cash flow with minimal investment
Convince competitor producers to fund industry-level advertising
Partner with cigar/premium lifestyle brands to boost fashion badge

recommendation: Recommend milking the brand as the primary strategy: given the sustained 3% annual volume decline in the overall scotch market, the economics of a turnaround investment are unfavorable — the advertising spend required to recover share would not be recouped over the remaining useful life of the brand
If the company wants to accelerate value capture, sell the brand now while it retains residual equity value, before further volume-driven erosion
risks: Milking the brand accelerates share loss, which may damage the parent company's relationships with distribution partners who carry the broader portfolio
If the super-premium and single malt segment continues to grow, exiting the scotch category entirely forfeits an option on segment recovery
Selling the brand may be difficult if potential acquirers also see the declining volume trend
risk: Milking accelerates share loss and may damage distributor relationships
Super-premium/single malt revival could make an early exit look premature
Brand sale may be difficult given visible volume decline trends
next_steps: Conduct a detailed brand valuation to set a floor price for a potential sale
Model the cash flows under a milk scenario (minimal advertising + cost reduction) versus a sell scenario to quantify the value difference
Explore whether industry-level advertising coalition with other producers is feasible to arrest category decline
